# Cisplatin: Comprehensive Safety Profile

## ⚠️ Overview

Cisplatin (*cis*-diamminedichloroplatinum II) is one of the most widely used cytotoxic agents, active against testicular, ovarian, bladder, lung, head & neck, and cervical cancers. Its clinical utility is constrained by a well-characterised, multi-organ toxicity profile. Acute toxicities — nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, and neurotoxicity — are dose-limiting and cause dose reductions, treatment delays, or cessation in **at least 30% of treated patients**. [^1^]

---

## 1. FDA Label: Principal Adverse Reactions & Frequencies

The FDA label identifies the following as the **five core adverse reactions** of cisplatin: nephrotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, nausea/vomiting, myelosuppression, and ototoxicity. [^2^]

| **Toxicity Domain** | **FDA-Label Frequency / Characteristics** |
|---|---|
| **Nephrotoxicity** | ~28–36% after a single 50 mg/m² dose; dose-related and cumulative; the **major dose-limiting toxicity**; onset typically in the 2nd week post-treatment |
| **Ototoxicity** | Up to ~31% after a single 50 mg/m² dose; cumulative, bilateral, progressive, irreversible sensorineural hearing loss (4,000–8,000 Hz); tinnitus; vestibular dysfunction; pediatric rates historically 40–60% |
| **Myelosuppression** | ~25–30%; leukopenia and thrombocytopenia; nadir days 18–23; recovery by ~day 39 |
| **Nausea/Vomiting** | **Almost all patients** without antiemetic prophylaxis; onset 1–4 h; may persist up to 72 h |
| **Peripheral Neuropathy** | Dose-related, cumulative; paresthesias, numbness, loss of vibration/position sense; onset typically 4–7 months; may be irreversible |
| **Hypersensitivity/Anaphylaxis** | Rare but potentially fatal; facial edema, bronchospasm, tachycardia, hypotension; may occur within minutes in previously exposed patients |
| **Electrolyte Disturbances** | Hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hyponatremia — secondary to renal tubular injury |
| **Ocular Toxicity** | Rare: optic neuritis, papilledema, cortical blindness, altered colour perception |

[^2^]

---

## 2. FAERS Disproportionality (PRR) — Signal Table

The most comprehensive published FAERS analysis (Feng et al., *Frontiers in Oncology*, 2023) mined Q1 2017–Q4 2021 data using PRR, ROR, and MHRA criteria, identifying **558 effective adverse event signals** for cisplatin across 23 system-organ classes (SOCs). [^3^] A complementary multi-database study (Nouth et al., *Current Science*, 2026) covering FAERS and EudraVigilance 2004–2025 provided additional nephrotoxicity-specific disproportionality values. [^4^]

> **Signal threshold:** PRR ≥ 2, ≥ 3 reports, chi-square ≥ 4 (standard MHRA criteria). A positive PRR indicates disproportionate reporting — **not proof of causation**.

### 2a. Nephrotoxicity Signals

| **MedDRA Preferred Term** | **PRR** | **ROR** | **Signal Strength** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nephropathy toxic | **20.52** | — | ⚫ Very strong | Strongest renal signal in Feng et al. 2023 [^3^] |
| Acute kidney injury (AKI) | **~5.14** | **5.05** | 🔴 Strong | Confirmed in both Feng et al. and Nouth et al. [^3^][^4^] |
| Renal salt-wasting syndrome (RSWS) | — | **481.57** | ⚫ Exceptional | Nouth et al. 2026; geriatric subgroup ROR = 737.90 [^4^] |
| Bladder necrosis / urinary tract structural damage | — | Significant | 🔴 Strong | Nouth et al. 2026 [^4^] |
| Increased serum creatinine / BUN | Positive | — | 🟡 Moderate | Consistent with label; Sakaeda et al. 2011 [^5^] |
| Hypomagnesemia / electrolyte disturbances | Positive | — | 🟡 Moderate | Renal tubular toxicity mechanism [^2^] |

**Temporal profile:** Nephrotoxicity signal in FAERS peaked in **2019**; median time-to-onset (TTO) = **10 days** (IQR 5–29 days); females had significantly shorter latency than males (9.5 vs. 11.0 days, p = 0.0289); 98.24% of reports were classified as **serious**. [^4^]

### 2b. Ototoxicity Signals

| **MedDRA Preferred Term** | **PRR / Signal** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|
| Sensorineural hearing loss | Positive signal | Confirmed in Feng et al. 2023 [^3^] |
| Mixed hearing loss / deafness | Positive signal | Confirmed in Feng et al. 2023 [^3^] |
| Tinnitus | Positive signal | Consistent with label; Sakaeda et al. 2011 [^5^] |
| High-frequency hearing impairment | Positive signal | 4,000–8,000 Hz range; label-consistent [^2^] |
| Vestibular toxicity | Positive signal | Dysequilibrium, vertigo [^6^] |

> ⚠️ **Note on PRR for ototoxicity:** The Feng et al. 2023 FAERS analysis confirmed cisplatin ototoxicity signals but did not publish individual PRR values per auditory preferred term in the available full text. A separate Canadian spontaneous-reporting analysis reported a cisplatin ototoxicity PRR of approximately **53.44**, but this is a non-FAERS (Health Canada) estimate and should not be conflated with U.S. FAERS values. [^3^]

### 2c. Other Major FAERS Signals (Feng et al. 2023)

| **SOC / Reaction** | **Signal** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|
| Febrile neutropenia | Positive | Dominant blood/lymphatic signal [^3^] |
| Nausea / vomiting | Positive | GI — most frequent AE category [^3^] |
| Peripheral neuropathy | Positive | Nervous system SOC [^3^][^5^] |
| Anaphylaxis / hypersensitivity | Positive | Administration-site / systemic reactions [^3^] |
| Thrombocytopenia / leukopenia | Positive | Myelosuppression cluster [^5^] |

---

## 3. Mechanism of Key Toxicities

### Nephrotoxicity
Cisplatin is actively taken up by renal proximal tubular cells via the organic cation transporter **OCT2** (encoded by *SLC22A2*) and the copper transporter **CTR1**. Intracellular accumulation triggers oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, and apoptosis/necrosis of tubular epithelium. [^7^] Sodium thiosulfate (STS) is believed to protect against nephrotoxicity by reducing cisplatin delivery to the kidneys and neutralising cisplatin within the renal parenchyma. [^6^]

### Ototoxicity
Cisplatin-induced hearing loss (CIHL) results from **irreversible damage to cochlear hair cells**, driven by oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. The cochlea is exquisitely sensitive to oxidative injury. STS protection involves: (i) binding to electrophilic platinum molecules, (ii) scavenging ROS, and (iii) increasing cochlear endolymph antioxidant concentrations. [^6^][^8^]

---

## 4. Pharmacogenomic Context

| **Gene / Variant** | **Toxicity** | **Evidence Level** | **Clinical Significance (2023–2024)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SLC22A2 / OCT2** | Nephrotoxicity | Moderate | Most clinically credible candidate; OCT2 mediates renal tubular cisplatin uptake; variants alter nephrotoxicity risk but **not yet practice-changing** [^9^] |
| **TPMT** | Ototoxicity | Moderate | Persisting signal; 2023 Canadian Pharmacogenomics Network review confirms TPMT and ACYP2 variants may identify higher-risk patients; **not yet universally implemented** [^9^] |
| **ACYP2 (rs1872328)** | Ototoxicity | Moderate | SNP associated with increased ototoxicity risk; referenced in patent literature for STS otoprotection eligibility [^6^] |
| **COMT** | Ototoxicity | Weak | Early candidate-gene association; **not consistently replicated** in large cohorts; current reviews de-emphasise it [^9^] |
| **LRP2 / Megalin** | Both | Weak | Biologically plausible (inner ear and renal tubular platinum handling); **not validated as a clinical decision marker** [^9^] |
| **TXNRD1** | Ototoxicity (hearing loss) | Exploratory | Borderline GWAS significance (p = 4.2×10⁻⁶) in testicular cancer survivors; redox regulation pathway [^10^] |
| **WNT8A** | Ototoxicity (tinnitus) | Exploratory | Gene-based GWAS signal (p = 2.5×10⁻⁶) in testicular cancer survivors [^10^] |
| **WFS1** | Ototoxicity | Exploratory | Marginal replication (p = 0.06) in independent cohort [^10^] |

> **Bottom line:** No CPIC-level prescribing guideline currently exists for cisplatin based on any of these variants. Routine genotype-guided cisplatin dosing is **not standard of care**. These markers serve primarily as **research/risk-stratification tools**. [^9^]

---

## 5. Clinical Trial & Literature Context

### Ototoxicity — Key Trial Evidence

| **Trial / Study** | **Key Finding** |
|---|---|
| **SIOPEL 6** (Phase III, Brock et al., *NEJM* 2018) | Sodium thiosulfate (STS) administered 6 h after cisplatin significantly reduced ototoxicity (Brock grade ≥1) in pediatric standard-risk hepatoblastoma; cisplatin efficacy was **not compromised** [^6^][^11^] |
| **COG ACCL0431** (Phase II, Freyer et al.) | STS reduced cisplatin-induced hearing loss in children; supported Phase III advancement [^11^] |
| **Decibel DB-020 Phase 1b** (2022) | Intratympanic STS formulation: 88% of placebo-treated ears experienced hearing loss vs. 87% partial/complete protection in treated ears; mild-to-moderate AEs only [^12^] |
| **Frisina et al., *JCO* 2016** | Comprehensive audiometric analysis in adult cisplatin survivors: significant rates of hearing impairment and tinnitus; underscores long-term burden [^11^] |
| **Rose et al., *Antioxidants* 2024** | State-of-the-art review: CIHL is bilateral, progressive, irreversible, dose-dependent; ~500,000 new cases of hearing loss per year from platinum-based chemotherapy globally; adult prevention remains an **unmet need** [^1^] |

### Nephrotoxicity — Key Trial/Literature Evidence

| **Study** | **Key Finding** |
|---|---|
| **Zhang et al., *Advances in Cancer Research* 2021** | Comprehensive review of cisplatin nephrotoxicity mechanisms: oxidative stress, inflammation, ER stress, transporter-mediated uptake (CTR1); multiple protective strategies reviewed [^7^] |
| **Nouth et al., *Current Science* 2026** | FAERS + EudraVigilance 2004–2025: 2,437 FAERS reports; 98.24% serious; RSWS signal (ROR = 481.57) is a **novel, underappreciated** nephrotoxicity phenotype beyond classic AKI; geriatric patients at highest risk [^4^] |
| **TOPAZ-1 (durvalumab + gemcitabine + cisplatin)** | Durvalumab did not add additional toxicity to gemcitabine/cisplatin backbone; cisplatin-related toxicities (including renal) were consistent with known profile [^13^] |

---

## 6. Otoprotection: Approved Intervention

Sodium thiosulfate (STS) is **FDA-approved** for the prevention of cisplatin-induced ototoxicity in **pediatric patients (≥1 month)** with localised, non-disseminated cancers. It is administered as a 15-minute IV infusion **6 hours after** completion of each cisplatin infusion (critical timing — earlier administration may reduce cisplatin efficacy). [^6^]

| **Body Weight** | **STS Dose** | **Volume** |
|---|---|---|
| >10 kg | 12.8 g/m² | 160 mL/m² |
| 5–10 kg | 9.6 g/m² | 120 mL/m² |
| <5 kg | 6.4 g/m² | 80 mL/m² |

[^6^]

> ⚠️ **Adult ototoxicity prevention remains an unmet clinical need** — no approved systemic otoprotectant exists for adults. [^1^]

---

## 7. Key Monitoring Recommendations (Label-Derived)

- **Renal:** Serum creatinine, BUN, eGFR, electrolytes (Mg²⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Na⁺) before each cycle
- **Auditory:** Audiometry at baseline and periodically; mandatory in children and patients receiving repeated doses
- **Haematologic:** CBC with differential and platelets before each cycle
- **Neurologic:** Symptom assessment for paresthesias, neuropathic pain
- **Hypersensitivity:** Emergency treatment capability must be immediately available during infusion [^2^]
